prize_parts.citation: For a visionary body of Romanian prose, rooted in poetry, that builds an encyclopedic, metaphysical architecture from memory, the body and dream, with rare formal ambition and imaginative depth.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: Cărtărescu alone, in one prize part. The chair's summary says that all six round-1 files point the same way, and I do not count that as merit. To test it, I tried to argue the strongest case for Carson, whom I ranked third, and then for Wright. Carson's formal invention and intellectual depth are real. Wright's polyphonic novels are a serious reinvention of the novel's idiom and scale. Neither case, as I can assess it, shows what the Cărtărescu case shows most clearly: a single imaginative project that is carried by the sentence and extended across a long career, from poetry to the Blinding trilogy and on to Solenoid. In that project memory, the body and dream recur and are rebuilt at larger scale. The voice is his own and rewards rereading, and none of this relies on topicality, nationality or political symbolism. What I have changed is the wording of the citation, not the writer. The chair asked whether prose only, prose and poetry, or prose with poetry as formative ground is the right scope. My answer is the third: the citation should rest on the prose, where the evidence is strongest, and should name the poetry as the root of the project rather than as a separately assessed body of work, because I cannot assess the poetry from translations. It should carry no regional or period label.
statement.case_against: My reservations stay the same, and I still cannot resolve them from general knowledge and translation. First, much of the achievement lies in Romanian syntax, rhythm and sonic patterning, so my judgment of the sentence is indirect. Second, the pattern-versus-overextension question cannot be settled without close reading of the whole corpus. In round 1 I leaned toward reading the recurring images as structure. That is an inference from public descriptions, and I should not present it as a finding. Third, the claim that the late novels extend the project and do not repeat it is, as Sem-Sandberg said, not settled by the supplied evidence. If close reading showed that the late volumes mostly repeat the earlier architecture, the sustained-quality criterion would weaken, and I would then move toward Carson's written lyric and essay work. Fourth, I have not independently verified any source, and the thin translation coverage of the poetry and early prose means a whole-oeuvre citation is only partly tested.

responses.point: Olsson moved Cărtărescu to first place and keeps Carson as the first alternative. He proposes that any Carson citation rest on her written lyric and essay work, with visual form as support. He also says her classical frame may limit her range, and that the 'idealistic tendency' in Nobel's will is open for her case.
responses.response: His proposal for narrowing a Carson citation is the fairest way to test her case, and I take it seriously. It does shrink the claim. Once Nox and the other book-objects are treated as support and the translations are set aside, what remains is a lyric and essay corpus that I know less well than the best-known hybrid works. I cannot show from public knowledge that this narrower body has the sustained quality across an oeuvre that a prize for a whole authorship requires. So I keep her as my first alternative, and the open question is evidence rather than a defect. On the will, I still do not think the 'idealistic tendency' wording separates the two cases. It is open for both writers, and I would not use it as a tie-breaker.

responses.point: Mattson asks whether the density of the late novels is purposeful pattern or overextension, and says only close reading of the whole corpus could settle it. She also says every other candidate faces a comparable limit of translation or compactness. She ranked Wright sixth and treats Wright's case as one of timing and breadth of corpus.
responses.response: I agree that the question cannot be settled by summary, and I would not offer more than a conditional answer. Her point that the other candidates face comparable limits is partly right. Carson's limit is material form and authorship scope, and Wright's is the number of major novels, so each is a limit of evidence and none is a ready reason to prefer another candidate. In round 1 I suggested that Carson and Wright might be less exposed to translation loss in English. I should qualify that. For Wright, the Aboriginal English and oral-form elements are exactly where I cannot judge detail, so her exposure is of a different kind rather than smaller. I do not hold the translation point as an argument against Cărtărescu in particular. I name it as an uncertainty for all three.

responses.point: Palm argues that the repeated images across volumes make length work as design rather than accumulation. She asks the citation to name the project, not each book, and says the thinner Wright corpus makes her case less complete rather than weaker in kind. She adds that a later round could revisit it.
responses.response: I share her reading of the repeated images, and I used the same reasoning in round 1. I now hold it more loosely. A recurring image can signal design, but it can also signal repetition, and public descriptions cannot tell me which holds for any given volume. Her suggestion that the citation name the project and not every book is the right answer to that. A citation then rests on the strongest sustained work and does not require every volume to be equal. On Wright I agree that the case is incomplete rather than weak in kind. The evidence that would move her from alternative to preferred is further major work, or close reading showing that the existing novels already deepen across the career. I cannot supply either from here, so I keep her as my second alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg says the supplied evidence does not settle whether the late Cărtărescu volumes extend or repeat the early project. He also says the question is best settled across the whole corpus, including poetry and shorter prose, and not by singling out the longest volumes. His alternatives are Murnane and Michon.
responses.response: He is right that I overreached in round 1 when I wrote that the long novels extend the project and do not simply repeat it. That is a plausible reading of public descriptions, not a verified finding, and I withdraw the firmer wording. His call to test the whole corpus is why I want the poetry named in the citation only as the root of the project. I cannot say which individual Orbitor volume is strongest or weakest. I can name only the structure of the trilogy and Solenoid as the evidence on which my view rests. As for his alternatives, Murnane's method is rigorous, but I share the doubt about development across the corpus. Michon's compact oeuvre makes significance across the body of work hard to establish, and I did not rank him in my top eight.

responses.point: Carlberg holds that the citation should not carry an 'Eastern European postmodern' label and that Cărtărescu's case is easier to define as one sustained imaginative project than Carson's. She holds that his metaphysical architecture engages Nobel's idealistic tendency more directly, which she calls her own reading and not a settled point.
responses.response: I agree on the label and on defining the project, and my revised wording reflects both. On the will, I treat her reading as a reasonable argument and not as a discriminating criterion. 'Idealistic' can be argued for a metaphysical prose project and also for a hybrid lyric and elegiac one, so I would not let it decide between B018 and B011. The weight of my preference falls on the other criteria: voice, formal achievement across large structures, and the coherence of the project.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's sentence-level rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning survives in translation is unresolved, and I cannot verify it. I name no specific Orbitor volume as strongest or weakest, because I lack a basis for ranking them.

Whether the late novels extend or partly repeat the earlier project remains open. A close reading of the whole corpus, including the poetry and shorter prose, could change my view and move me toward Carson.
Coverage of the poetry and early prose in translation is thin, so the roots-in-poetry wording in the citation is cautious and the whole-oeuvre claim is only partly tested.

For Carson, I cannot say how much of the written lyric and essay corpus, apart from the book-objects and translations, carries sustained quality, nor how the authorship scope would be fixed. For Wright, a small number of major novels limits what I can say about sustained quality and growth, and I cannot judge the Aboriginal English and oral-form elements in detail.

My assessments rest on public knowledge and the supplied shortlist descriptions, not on close reading or independent verification. The simulation models a committee recommendation, and the full Swedish Academy makes any actual award decision.
statement.conflict_note: No personal, professional or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer appears in my supplied profile, and I request no recusal. For transparency, I disclose the following context only. My profile records a 2021 public statement that the Academy has missed many major female authorships and that she values a female perspective in an international prize. I do not treat it as evidence of a preference for or against any shortlisted writer, and my preference here rests on the common literary criteria. My own practice as a novelist is also context, not a reason for preferring a candidate. These disclosures are not adjudicated here.
